name: Tomas Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the press line at a washing machine factory, the big one by the motorway junction. We take rolls of steel, and the presses stamp out the side panels and the drum parts, bang, bang, all day. I load the coils, set the press for each model, check the first panels with a gauge and keep things moving, and there's a robot arm that moves the panels between presses already. I like the crew and the feeling of a good, fast run. What wears me out is the noise, and the night shifts every third week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside the factory, what's your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, she teaches seven-year-olds. We rent a nice place near the river, and I own a small studio flat across town that I bought with money my grandad left me, which I rent out to a student. I've got about a year of expenses saved. We're talking about getting married, maybe next summer, if we can agree on the guest list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that noise and it's a better spellchecker. I'd probably joke about it in the group chat with the lads from football. Nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be good news. I like my job well enough, the pay's good, and I've got a plan. I'd rather argue with Ana about the wedding guest list than about whether I still have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep the studio rented, keep saving, set a date for the wedding and book the hall by the river. Maybe ask about the setter role on the press line, which pays a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to check the rental contract for the studio, and Ana uses it to make worksheets. At work, not really, the robot arm's been there for years and it's not exactly clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you go for the setter role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the money and a bit less lifting. The setter, Hugo, is retiring next year. I've been watching how he does it, so I think I'd have a decent shot.

S0.say: I'd joke that all that noise came down to a better spellchecker. I'd laugh about it in the football group chat and leave it there.
S0.think: Honestly, it'd be good news, because I like my job, the pay's good and I've got a plan. I'd rather argue with Ana about the guest list than about my job.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, keeps the studio rented and keeps saving. Sets a wedding date, books the hall and applies for the setter role when the current setter retires.
S0.quote: I'd rather argue with Ana about the wedding guest list than about whether I still have a job.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is relaxed, sociable and comfortable, with a rental flat and a year's savings. He uses AI occasionally for practical things outside work. His ambitions are modest and well within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense, companies have to keep up or they lose to the ones that do. But I'd also say the government needs to help people retrain, because not everyone can switch overnight. Middle of the road, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit worried. They'd automate the coil loading and the gauge checks first, that's half of what I do. But if there's a few years, I'd probably move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the company does and what the other plants do. If they start using AI for the press settings, I'd make sure I learn it early, maybe practise at home with the tools. I wouldn't jump to anything else until I saw what was actually happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before you'd act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A new machine on the floor, or a memo about it. I'm not going to retrain because of a headline, but I will if a crate turns up with a robot in it. That's how I've always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. Steady change is just life. We'd still book the hall, maybe spend a bit less on the band.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense for companies to keep up, but the government needs to help people retrain because not everyone can switch overnight.
S1.think: I'd be a bit worried, because coil loading and gauge checks are half my job and easy to automate. But with a few years, I'd probably move with it.
S1.do: Watches what his company and other plants do, and learns any new AI press-setting tools early, practising at home. Waits for real changes on the floor before making any bigger moves.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like waiting for exam results.
S1.quote: I'm not going to retrain because of a headline, but I will if a crate turns up with a robot in it.
S1.fieldNote: Tomas waits for proof before acting, and he has a clear trigger in a new machine arriving. He sees both sides on who should adapt, companies and government. The wedding goes ahead in this picture, only a little cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody was ready for this and that's a failure all round, the companies for rushing it and the government for sleeping. I'd say we need emergency help for workers, now. I'd probably say it more angrily than I normally talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the press line goes first. Robots already move the panels, so it'd be a short step to robots doing everything. In two years I'd be out, and so would every other press operator nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could and cut back hard, no new car, nothing. I'd talk to Ana about pushing the wedding back, because I don't want to spend our savings on a party if I don't have a job. The studio rent would become really important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel a bit sick about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we should wait a year on the wedding, and I'd feel awful saying it. She'd say a wedding doesn't need a job, and I'd say no, but the band does. We'd laugh, but it'd be a sad laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Is there any training you'd try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look, but I'd be guessing. If AI can do almost anything, then I'd just be picking which job dies second. I'd rather keep the money safe and wait to see what's left.

S2.say: I'd say nobody was ready and that's a failure all round, by companies rushing it and governments sleeping. Workers need emergency help now.
S2.think: I think the press line would go first, because robots already move the panels between presses. Within two years I'd be out, and so would every other press operator nearby.
S2.do: Saves everything and cuts back hard, including dropping plans for a new car. Asks Ana to postpone the wedding and relies more on rent from the studio.
S2.feel: Alarmed and a bit sick about it.
S2.quote: She'd say a wedding doesn't need a job, and I'd say no, but the band does.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI hits Tomas where it matters most to him, the wedding. He becomes angrier than his centrist manner usually allows. The rental studio becomes his lifeline, and he chooses to hold cash rather than gamble on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be sensible. The companies should give notice, and the government should fund training for people who need it. I wouldn't be shouting, I'd be planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to do something. I'd think about which jobs need hands in odd places, like fitting heat pumps in old houses. Robots might get there in the end, but every house is a mess in its own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in heating and heat pump installation, two nights a week. I'd keep working the presses for the money. We'd still get married, but maybe a smaller do, and I'd keep the studio as backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind where you get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots might get there in the end. Why train for it, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it buys me years. If the factory goes in five, maybe houses go in eight or ten. Three extra years of wages is three extra years of not touching the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to try before I jump. I could do some weekend jobs with a friend who installs boilers and see if I actually like it, before I quit the factory. With two years, I'd have had to guess.

S3.say: I'd say we have time, so let's be sensible: companies should give notice and the government should fund training for those who need it.
S3.think: Five years is enough to move into work that needs hands in awkward places, like fitting heat pumps in old houses. I think robots would get there later than they get to the factory.
S3.do: Starts a two-nights-a-week heating and heat pump installation course in the first year while still working the presses. Gets married with a smaller wedding and keeps the studio as a backup.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a get-on-with-it way.
S3.quote: Three extra years of wages is three extra years of not touching the savings.
S3.fieldNote: Tomas uses the extra time to test a new trade before leaving, which is classic steady behaviour. He's realistic that it only buys a few years. The wedding survives, scaled down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out if they start early. I'd tell the younger guys at the plant to pick something now. And I'd say the government should help with the cost of training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels fine for me. I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe a kid. I'd have time to change trade and build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the heating course in the first two years and switch jobs around year three. I'd keep saving and maybe buy a second small flat to rent out, because people will still need somewhere to live. We'd get married next summer as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy another flat, if the economy might change so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust anything else. Shares go up and down, but a flat is four walls and a roof, and even a robot can't take that away from you. It might be wrong, but it feels solid to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at work struggle with the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the older guys who are fifty-five now. They'd be sixty-five when it lands, so they might just make it to retirement. It's the ones in their forties I'd worry about, with kids and mortgages.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for most people to sort themselves out if they start early, and I'd tell younger colleagues to pick something now. The government should help pay for training.
S4.think: Ten years feels fine for me. I'd be thirty-seven, married and maybe with a kid, and I'd have time to change trade and build something.
S4.do: Takes the heating course in the first two years and switches jobs around year three. Keeps saving, buys a second small rental flat and marries next summer as planned.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than worried.
S4.quote: a flat is four walls and a roof, and even a robot can't take that away from you.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Tomas returns almost to his normal plans, adding a second rental flat as security. His faith in property is emotional rather than analytical, and he admits it. He thinks of colleagues in their forties with families as the ones most at risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits everything at once: the job, the wedding, the plans. I can change trade, but not in eighteen months, and not while I'm getting married. What would help is the government paying people a wage while they retrain, so you can learn without spending all your savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it changes the way people plan their lives, not just jobs. Me and Ana talk about kids, about a house. All that depends on knowing roughly what the next ten years look like.

headlineQuote: I can change trade, but not in eighteen months, and not while I'm getting married.
portrait: Tomas is a 27-year-old press operator at a washing machine factory, living with his teacher girlfriend Ana and owning a small rental studio bought with his grandfather's money. He's sociable, practical and centrist, using AI now and then for everyday tasks. He waits for real proof before acting, staying calm in the plateau but becoming alarmed by fast AGI, which would make him postpone his wedding. With five or ten years he plans to retrain as a heat pump installer and buy another rental flat, trusting bricks more than anything else.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most because it would hit his job, wedding and plans all at once, with no time to change trade.
whatWouldHelp: Government paying people a wage while they retrain, so they can learn without using up their savings.
